summary:
Article 567 of the Penal Code criminalises sexual relations with a person of the same sex and applies to conduct by both men and women. The provision was passed on 22 November 2008 and took effect on 22 April 2009; such conduct was not criminalised before that date. The penalty is three months to two years imprisonment and a fine of 50,000 to 100,000 Burundian francs. Reporting by OutRight International as of March 2026 instead cites Article 250 of the Penal Code for the same offence, with up to two years in prison and a fine; the two article numbers are not reconciled in the sources.

Burundi provides no legal gender recognition as of March 2026, so a visitor cannot obtain local documents or markers matching their gender. LGBTIQ organisations cannot register as associations, which removes the ordinary route to formal protection or collective redress.

Article 29 of the Constitution bans same-sex marriage, and neither same-sex marriage nor civil unions are recognised. A trans visitor whose partnership would be read under their document status as a same-sex union has no route to recognition of it in Burundi.

Enforcement is documented in discrete cases across the country. A man in Bujumbura was arrested on 1 July 2009 on suspicion of being gay, with police offering release in exchange for money, and he was released after advocacy. Two women were briefly arrested and released in 2012. In September 2014 a case in Karuzi Province involving a Viettel employee and a Burundian man was dropped after three days for lack of evidence. On 2 November 2016 the High Court of Cibitoke Province sentenced a 15-year-old boy who admitted raping a seven-year-old boy to one year in prison on charges of rape of a minor and homosexuality. In March 2023, 24 people were arrested on same-sex conduct charges; the accused were acquitted on that charge after one accused person died in detention, while seven received convictions for inciting debauchery. In August 2023, seven people were sentenced to one to two years in prison for engaging in homosexual acts. The most recent documented sentencing in this record is from August 2023, and no later instance is documented. A 2016 US State Department report recorded no prosecutions during that year.

Official hostility is on the record. In December 2023 President Évariste Ndayishimiye compared gay sex to choosing Satan and said people found engaging in it should be taken to stadiums and stoned; he also rejected foreign aid conditioned on respecting LGBT rights. Human Rights Watch reported in January 2024 on the call to 'stone' homosexuals and urged the ruling party to renounce persecution. The Iteka League, operating in exile, described the remarks as a call for the lynching of LGBTQ people, and members of two LGBTQ associations told SOS Médias Burundi anonymously that the remarks amounted to a real license to kill. The most recent documented official statement in this record is from December 2023, reported in January 2024, and no later instance is documented.

US State Department human-rights reports covering 2009, 2010, 2012 and 2015 document discrimination against gays and lesbians among the country's routine abuses, alongside arrests and harassment of LGBT persons under the criminalised framework. The 2016 report states that LGBT persons faced societal discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity with no government protection from it. OutRight International reports, as of March 2026, high levels of harassment, discrimination, family rejection and stigmatisation affecting LGBTIQ people, with no meaningful legal reform.
tangentialFactors:
The documented enforcement cases cluster around charges laid alongside other offences, including rape of a minor in Cibitoke Province in November 2016 and inciting debauchery in the March 2023 proceedings, which produced convictions even where the same-sex conduct charge itself was dropped after an accused person died in detention. A visitor should expect prosecution to be pursued through whatever charge will hold.

The same US State Department reporting that records LGBT discrimination also records a wider crisis of state conduct, including extrajudicial killings, arbitrary detention, torture, harsh prison conditions, prolonged pretrial detention and media shutdowns, documented for 2010, 2012 and 2015. Where state agencies are themselves the source of such abuse, a complaint about extortion or arbitrary arrest carries less practical weight than the arrest record alone would suggest. The 2009 Bujumbura case, in which police offered release for money, illustrates that dynamic directly.

The constitutional prohibition in Article 29 forecloses legislative change through the ordinary route, and the March 2026 position on gender recognition and association registration shows no reform movement on either front. Where the 2009, 2012, 2014 and 2016 cases ended in release, acquittal or dropped charges, the March 2023 and August 2023 proceedings ended in convictions and custodial sentences of one to two years.
localsOnly:
Residents have no mechanism for legal gender recognition as of March 2026, so Burundian trans people carry documents that do not match their gender, with knock-on effects for every interaction that checks identity papers.

LGBTIQ organisations cannot register as associations, which leaves residents without a legally constituted body to advocate for them, provide services or bring complaints. The Iteka League operates from exile and has no standing inside the country.

Family rejection, stigmatisation, harassment and discrimination are reported by OutRight International as the prevailing condition for LGBTIQ Burundians as of March 2026, compounding the criminal exposure under the Penal Code. Two associations surveyed after the December 2023 presidential remarks described their members as being in a state of terror, and one called the remarks a license to kill.

Custodial sentences handed to residents run from one to two years, as in the August 2023 case of seven people, with the added exposure of fines of 50,000 to 100,000 francs under Article 567. The March 2023 proceedings show that a group arrest can produce convictions on ancillary charges even when the conduct charge fails.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources give two different article numbers for the same offence: Article 567 in the 2008 enactment and in reporting through 2016, and Article 250 in OutRight International's March 2026 material. Whether this reflects a renumbering, a recodification or a citation error is unresolved in this inventory.

The inventory contains no incident documented as targeting a person specifically for being transgender rather than for same-sex conduct; the charged cases all turn on the same-sex conduct provisions. How Article 567 or Article 250 would be applied to a trans visitor whose documents and presentation differ is not sourced here.

Entry, visa and border-screening treatment of transgender travellers in Burundi is not covered by any source in this inventory, including whether passport markers or gender presentation trigger secondary examination at Bujumbura or other ports of entry. Access to hormone therapy, trans-specific healthcare and detention-placement rules by gender are likewise not sourced.

Whether foreign same-sex marriages are consulted or recognised in any administrative proceeding, beyond the constitutional ban on entering one locally, is unresolved here.
